passage:
In Nairobi, Wanjiru hugged her little brother Sami after he cried over her new crayons. "I promise I'll share them forever and ever," she said, and she meant it with her whole body.
The next morning Sami reached for the purple one. Wanjiru snatched the box. "Mine!"
"You promised," Sami wailed.
Wanjiru looked confused, then cross, then sad. Yesterday's promise felt very far away. Mama knelt down. "Promises are for tomorrow-you too," she said softly. "Shall we choose which colours Sami can use today?"

qa.q: What did Wanjiru promise Sami?
qa.a: Wanjiru promised to share the crayons forever and ever.

qa.q: How did Wanjiru feel when Sami said "You promised"?
qa.a: She felt confused, then cross, then sad, because yesterday's promise felt very far away.

qa.q: How did Mama help Wanjiru keep her promise?
qa.a: Mama knelt down, gently explained that promises are for tomorrow-you too, and helped her choose some colours to share today.

qa.q: What is it like for Sami when Wanjiru snatches the box?
qa.a: Sami feels let down and upset, because he trusted the promise she made yesterday.

grounding: A young girl promises to share forever and means it, but does not yet understand that the promise binds her the next day too.

passage:
In the nursery class, Omkar stood at the door with wet cheeks. Yesterday, at home time, he had told Jomon Sir, "Tomorrow I won't cry. Pinky promise!" He had hooked his little finger tight, very serious.
But this morning Amma turned to go, and the crying came anyway, big and loud. Between sobs he said, "But I... promised." He looked shocked at himself.
Jomon Sir crouched beside him. "You meant it yesterday, and that was brave. Today's feelings are big. Let's hold hands at the window and wave." Omkar sniffled, held on, and waved.

qa.q: What did Omkar promise Jomon Sir at home time?
qa.a: Omkar said, "Tomorrow I won't cry. Pinky promise!"

qa.q: Why did Omkar look shocked at himself?
qa.a: He had meant the promise fully and didn't expect the crying to come anyway, so breaking it surprised and upset him.

qa.q: What did Jomon Sir do that helped?
qa.a: He praised Omkar for meaning it, named today's big feelings, and gave a small plan to hold hands and wave.

qa.q: How might Amma feel as she turns to go?
qa.a: She may feel sad to see him cry, and relieved that Jomon Sir is there to comfort him.

grounding: A small boy makes a serious promise not to cry, meaning it fully, and is surprised when tomorrow's feelings are different.

passage:
Pranav held the new crayon box with both hands in the stationery shop.
"Only if you share with Sabina," Mumma said.
"I promise! I promise, promise!" He meant every word.
At home, his little sister Sabina reached for the red crayon. Pranav pulled the box to his chest. "No! Mine!"
"But you promised," Mumma said softly.
Pranav's lip wobbled. In the shop, sharing had felt easy. Now the red crayon felt like everything.
Mumma sat beside him. "Promises are hard when the feeling changes, na? Let's give Sabina two colours to start."
Slowly, Pranav held out the blue and the green.

qa.q: Which crayon did Sabina reach for?
qa.a: Sabina reached for the red crayon.

qa.q: Why did Pranav's lip wobble?
qa.a: Pranav felt sad and torn, because he had meant his promise in the shop but now wanted to keep the red crayon.

qa.q: How did Mumma help Pranav keep his promise?
qa.a: She stayed gentle, named that promises are hard when feelings change, and suggested a small start of two colours.

qa.q: How does Sabina experience the moment Pranav shouts "Mine"?
qa.a: Sabina is probably surprised and upset, since she expected to share the new crayons.

grounding: It shows a young child promising to share with full sincerity and then struggling when his later self feels differently.

passage:
"Sumit, can you tidy the blocks after you play?"
"Yes, Papa! I promise!"
"And Abhinav, you'll help your brother?"
"I promise too!"
Later, blocks everywhere. Sumit lay on the sofa.
"Sumit, you promised."
"I'm tired, Papa."
"But you said you would."
"That was before. I wasn't tired before." Sumit's eyes filled with tears.
Abhinav picked up two blocks. "I promised too."
Papa knelt down. "When you promise, it's also for later-you. Tired Sumit has to do what happy Sumit said."
Sumit sniffed. "Can tired Sumit do only the red ones?"
Papa smiled. "Tired Sumit can start with the red ones."

qa.q: What did Sumit promise to do after playing?
qa.a: He promised to tidy the blocks.

qa.q: Why did Sumit's eyes fill with tears?
qa.a: Sumit felt tired and sad, and confused that the promise he meant earlier now felt too hard.

qa.q: How did Papa help Sumit understand promises?
qa.a: Papa explained kindly that a promise is also for "later-you" and let him start small with the red ones.

qa.q: What is it like for Abhinav when Sumit won't tidy?
qa.a: Abhinav wants to keep that promise too and feels a little proud picking up blocks, even when Sumit lies on the sofa.

grounding: It shows small children promising to tidy up and meaning it, then finding the later tired self feels differently.

passage:
Nursery class note to parents, Tuesday.
At the gate this morning, Swati hugged her Mumma and said very seriously, "I promise I won't cry today." She meant it fully.
When the gate closed, her face crumpled. "But I promised," she sobbed, and cried harder.
Sharmila, who sits next to her, came and held her hand without a word. I told Swati, "Missing Mumma is okay. Feelings can change even after we promise."
Soon she was playing at the sand tray with Sharmila. At home, you might promise something small together instead, like one big hug at the gate.

qa.q: What did Swati promise her Mumma at the gate?
qa.a: She said, "I promise I won't cry today."

qa.q: Why did Swati cry harder after saying "But I promised"?
qa.a: Swati felt sad and worried that she had broken her promise, on top of missing Mumma.

qa.q: What did the teacher suggest to the parents?
qa.a: The teacher suggested promising something small together at home, like one big hug at the gate.

qa.q: How might Sharmila have felt when she held Swati's hand?
qa.a: Sharmila probably felt caring and a little worried for her friend, so she offered comfort without words.

grounding: A nursery teacher notes a small child who fully meant her promise not to cry and was upset when her feelings changed later.

passage:
At the Onam gathering in their small town near Thrissur, Gopika clutched her new doll. Her cousin Parul was crying because she wanted a turn.
"I promise I'll share after lunch!" Gopika said, very seriously. Parul stopped crying.
After lunch, Parul held out her hands. Gopika hugged the doll tighter. "No. She's sleeping."
Parul's lip wobbled again.
Amma knelt beside Gopika. "You promised, remember? Promises are for later-you too." Gopika frowned, thinking hard about later-her. Then, slowly, she held out the doll for a short turn.

qa.q: When did Gopika promise to share the doll?
qa.a: After lunch.

qa.q: What did Gopika feel after lunch when Parul held out her hands?
qa.a: Gopika felt stubborn and possessive, hugging the doll tighter; the promise had felt real before lunch, but now she felt different.

qa.q: How did Amma help Gopika keep the promise?
qa.a: Amma knelt beside her and gently reminded her that promises are for later-you too, letting Gopika choose to give a short turn.

qa.q: How did Parul feel when Gopika said 'She's sleeping'?
qa.a: Parul's lip wobbled; she felt let down and close to tears again.

grounding: Shows a young child promising to share and meaning it fully, then finding the later self feels differently.
